description: Dedicated reference entries for ship detection methods, evasion, pursuit, and interception.

entries.title: Visual Ship Tracking
entries.summary: Smoke, reflected light, disturbed clouds, and direct observation can reveal a vessel without specialized equipment.
body: Visual tracking relies on signs left in open sky: smoke, glints from hull or glass, altered cloud patterns, and a visible silhouette. Weather, darkness, wind, distance, and terrain can strengthen or erase those signs.
A smoke trail is easy to begin following under favorable conditions but may disperse or become confused with environmental haze.

sections.heading: Legacy Visual Tracking
body: The source assigns Perception checks, timed pursuit rolls, distance modifiers, and wind effects. These numerical procedures require conversion.

sourceRefs.outlineTitle: Tracking a Ship / Visual Tracking and Smoke Cloud

entries.title: Ether Trail Tracking
entries.summary: Arcane observers can follow magical emissions and elemental disturbances left by an airship core.
body: Ether trails provide a magical path when ordinary sight is unreliable. The strength of a ship's output determines how obvious the trail is, while dampened regions and magical interference can obscure it.
Stealth runes and related concealment measures can deliberately weaken the signature, requiring trackers to distinguish the target from ambient aetheric activity.

sections.heading: Legacy Ether Tracking
body: The source assigns Arcana checks, timed pursuit rolls, range modifiers, and stealth-rune effects. These numerical procedures require conversion.

entries.title: Radar and Sonar Ship Tracking
entries.summary: Mechanical sensors locate vessels through instrument readings but remain vulnerable to range, clouds, and magical interference.
body: Radar, sonar, thermal systems, and related devices shift tracking from direct observation to investigation of sensor returns. Higher-quality systems extend useful detection and improve the detail available to operators.
Dense clouds and magical disruption can conceal or distort a target. Trained sensor operators are therefore as important as the equipment itself.

sections.heading: Legacy Sensor Tracking
body: The source assigns Investigation checks, equipment-quality modifiers, timed pursuit rolls, and cloud or magical-interference penalties. These numerical procedures require conversion.

entries.title: Ship Tracking and Evasion
entries.summary: Targets break pursuit through maneuvering, cloud cover, storms, stealth conditions, and magical concealment.
body: A tracked vessel can make itself harder to follow by changing course aggressively, entering dense weather, concealing its magical signature, or using illusion and invisibility.

Tracking ships counter evasion through better sensors, trained mages or operators, and simultaneous use of visual, magical, and mechanical methods. Distance and prolonged pursuit gradually favor the escaping vessel.

sections.heading: Legacy Evasion Modifiers
body: The source provides pilot checks, tracking-DC increases, concealment checks, equipment bonuses, and multi-method advantage. These numerical procedures require conversion.

sourceRefs.outlineTitle: Tracking a Ship / Evasion and Tracker Modifiers

entries.title: Prolonged Ship Pursuit
entries.summary: Long chases strain crews and equipment, while teamwork and multiple trackers can preserve a fading trail.
body: Extended pursuit becomes harder as fatigue, equipment strain, distance, and environmental interference accumulate. Exceptional observations may reveal heading, speed, and vessel type, while a serious mistake can lose the trail entirely.
Multiple allied trackers can compare methods and recover from individual failures. Stealth-equipped targets still impose a major obstacle unless the pursuit force carries appropriate countermeasures.

sections.heading: Legacy Advanced Tracking
body: The source defines critical results, hourly difficulty increases, reacquisition time, teamwork rerolls, and stealth penalties. These numerical procedures require conversion.

entries.title: Ship Interception
entries.summary: A successful track becomes an interception only after the pursuer closes distance and defeats the target's piloting response.
body: Maintaining a trail provides periodic location and heading updates but does not by itself bring two ships together. The pursuer must close the gap while the target continues to maneuver or seek cover.

Once close enough, opposed piloting determines whether the pursuer can engage, board, or force the target into ship-to-ship combat. Repeated failed tracking attempts can end the chase before interception becomes possible.

sections.heading: Legacy Interception Procedure
body: The source defines consecutive-failure loss, a one-mile interception threshold, and opposed pilot checks. These numerical procedures require conversion.
